newsitem.title: FRANCE: French rivals spar over tv debate in tight race.
newsitem.headline: French rivals spar over tv debate in tight race.

text.p: French political leaders played cat-and-mouse on Friday over a television debate as the campaign for a snap parliamentary election looked increasingly risky for President Jacques Chirac's centre-right government.

Opposition Socialist leader Lionel Jospin, buoyed by a poll suggesting left and right are neck-and-neck, rejected a four-way debate with leaders of other parliamentary parties and challenged Prime Minister Alain Juppe to a one-on-one showdown.

Juppe, centre-right UDF party leader Francois Leotard and Communist leader Robert Hue all said they had accepted the private TF1 channel's invitation for a four-way debate on May 20, five days before the first round of voting.

But Jospin said on a campaign trip to Toulouse in southern France: "I don't understand why Alain Juppe is rushing to a four-way formula. It is as if he needed a second because he is scared of a direct confrontation with me.
"He prefers doubles but I play singles and, in politics, you've got to be straight, clear and defend your positions," the Socialist leader said.

The shadow-boxing reflected both the Socialists' drive to focus the campaign on Juppe's unpopular record and personality, and the ruling coalition's effort to depict Jospin as dependent on the Communists for a parliamentary majority.
A four-way debate would be likely to highlight differences between the Socialists and Communists on the key issue of a single European currency.
Opinion pollsters said the race seemed extremely tight and public opinion was very volatile.

An IPSOS opinion poll taken on Tuesday and Wednesday found the ruling coalition would win 292 seats in the 577-member National Assembly, just three more than the 289 required for a majority, with the opposition Socialists taking 256, the Communists 28 and the far-right National Front one.
"Statistically speaking, they (the majority and the Left) are level," Pierre Giacometti of IPSOS told Reuters. "But what was true yesterday is no longer true today."
Thirty-one percent of voters questioned did not state their voting intention, and almost 40 percent of those who did said they might still change their minds.
Giacometti said that according to his institute's model some 180 seats hung on a margin of less than five percentage points.
Rumours that polls yet to be published showed the left with a slight lead caused the franc, interest rate futures and shares to fall on French financial markets on Friday, dealers said.

Taking to the hustings for the first time since President Jacques Chirac dissolved parliament on Monday, Juppe accused the Socialists on Thursday night of betraying their European ideals and planning archaic tax-and-spend policies.

"The Socialists, powerfully aided by their Communist allies, without whose votes they have no hope of a majority, have got the wrong century," Juppe told a rally in Marseille. "You wonder whether they see the world as it is."
Speaking at the same rally, Leotard also played up the theme of the "Socialo-Communist" threat which dominated French election campaigns of the 1970s and 1980s.
"Every time Mr Jospin depicts us as harsh capitalists, we will call them the Marxists they really are," he said.

Partly in an attempt to forge an electoral pact with the Communists, whom he is due to meet next Tuesday, Jospin has posed conditions for a single European currency, ruling out further austerity to prepare for the euro.

He told a campaign rally in Sarcelles on Thursday night he wanted the euro "but not a euro confiscated by the financial markets. We don't want an euro that would force Europe to pursue deflationary, economic stagnation policies".
